Understanding Your Time

Before you can plan well, you need an honest picture of where your hours go. In this module you count the hours in your week, run a seven-day time audit, find the habits and situations that drain your time and energy, and build the first small habits of taking charge.
Your 168-Hour Week: Fixed Time, Flexible Time and Energy

Separate fixed time from flexible time in your own week
Explain why energy matters as much as hours
Describe the difference between a reactive day and a planned day

Every week has exactly **168 hours** (7 days x 24 hours). Nobody gets more. What differs from one woman to another is how much of that time is already spoken for, and how much is left for the things she chooses. This lesson helps you see your week as a set of numbers you can work with, instead of a blur of tiredness.
A woman standing beside a large clock and a calendar
Seeing your week as 168 hours turns a vague feeling of having no time into numbers you can plan with.
Fixed time and flexible time

**Fixed time** is time you cannot easily move: sleep, your job or shop hours, the school run, travel in traffic, cooking the main meal, worship services you attend every week. **Flexible time** is everything else: scrolling, visiting, extra chores, rest, learning, side projects. Most women discover that their flexible time is smaller than they hoped, but also larger than it feels, because much of it leaks away in small pieces of 10 and 20 minutes.
**Sleep:** most adults need 7 or more hours a night, so plan about 49 to 56 hours a week.
**Work or business:** shop hours, office hours, or the time you spend producing and delivering goods.
**Travel:** school runs, going to market, commuting. In big cities like Lagos or Abuja this can be 10 or more hours a week.
**Home basics:** cooking, washing up, laundry, fetching or storing water, cleaning.
**Care:** bathing small children, homework help, caring for an elderly parent.
Worked example: counting a real week
For example, Ngozi runs a small provisions shop in Enugu and has two children in primary school. She writes down her fixed hours with a pencil.
Sleep: 7 hours x 7 nights = 49 hours.
Shop: 9 hours x 6 days = 54 hours.
School run and market trips: about 1.5 hours x 6 days = 9 hours.
Cooking, washing up and laundry: about 2.5 hours x 7 days = 17.5 hours.
Church on Sunday and midweek service: about 5 hours.
Total fixed time: 49 + 54 + 9 + 17.5 + 5 = 134.5 hours. Flexible time: 168 minus 134.5 = 33.5 hours.
Ngozi has about 33 flexible hours a week, roughly 4 to 5 hours a day. She had believed she had none. Now she can decide what those hours are for.
Hours are not all equal: energy

An hour at 6 am after good sleep is not the same as an hour at 10 pm after a long day in the shop. Your **energy** rises and falls during the day. Many people think most clearly in the morning, but some are sharper later. Notice when you feel alert and when you feel drained. Use your best-energy hours for work that needs thinking (accounts, planning, learning, important conversations) and your low-energy hours for simple tasks (folding clothes, sorting beans, replying to easy messages).
Find your best hours
For three days, write a number from 1 (exhausted) to 5 (fresh and focused) next to each two-hour block of your day. Look for the pattern. Protect your 4s and 5s for your most important tasks.
Reactive days and planned days

A **reactive** day is run by whatever shouts loudest: a phone call, a neighbour at the gate, a customer on WhatsApp, a child who suddenly needs something for school tomorrow. A **planned** day still has surprises, but you have already decided your top tasks and left some space for interruptions. You do not need to plan every minute. Even deciding three things the night before changes how the day feels.

Common mindsets that shrink your time
**'I have no time.'** Said often, it stops you looking for the hours you do have. Replace it with 'This is not a priority this week', which is usually more honest.
**Busyness as proof of worth.** Being seen to rush about can feel like being a good wife, mother or worker. But busy and effective are different things.
**Perfectionism.** Spending an hour making something perfect when ten minutes would make it good enough. Ask: what level of quality does this task really need?
**Saying yes to everyone.** Every yes to someone else uses hours from your 168. You will learn kind ways to say no in Module 2.
None of these mindsets make you a bad person; they are common habits of thinking. Simply noticing which one you fall into most is the first step to changing it.

The Seven-Day Time Audit: Where Your Hours Really Go

Group your activities into clear categories and total them

In the last lesson you estimated your week. Estimates are useful, but memory is not reliable: we forget the 20 minutes spent searching for keys or the hour that disappeared on WhatsApp statuses. A **time audit** means writing down what you actually did, as you go, for one full week. It is the single most useful thing you can do before making any plan.
A stopwatch
A time audit measures your real week, in small blocks, instead of relying on memory.
How to run the audit
Choose a normal week, not a festive season or a week when you are travelling.
Prepare a log: a notebook page per day with times down the side from waking to sleeping, in 30-minute rows. A phone notes app works too.
Every two or three hours, stop and fill in what you did in each 30-minute block. Do not wait until night.
Be honest. Write 'phone, TikTok' or 'chatting with neighbour' if that is what happened. Nobody else needs to see it.
At the end of each day, mark each block with a category letter.

She decides on one change: no social media before her baking orders are done, using an app timer.
By acting on one clear finding, Halima wins back several hours a week for her cake orders without giving up her phone completely.

Common surprises
Phone time is usually two to three times higher than people guess.
Waiting (queues, power cuts, late visitors) adds up to more than expected. Waiting time can be used for small tasks like planning or reading.
Small unplanned market trips (for one missing item) cost a lot of travel time. A weekly list fixes much of this.
Rest is often almost missing. That is a warning sign, not a badge of honour.
Be kind to yourself
The audit is information, not a judgement. Its purpose is to show you where change is possible. Many women find that just keeping the log makes them use time more carefully during that week.

Also look at the **shape** of your days, not only the totals. Are mornings calm and evenings chaotic, or the other way round? Is Saturday overloaded with all the cleaning, laundry and visits? Which day of the week is lightest? These patterns tell you where to place important tasks when you plan your week in Module 2.
If a full week feels too much

If seven days of logging feels impossible, log three days: two weekdays and one weekend day. The picture will be less complete but still useful. Another option is to set a phone alarm every two hours labelled 'log', so you remember. If you cannot read or write easily, you can record a short voice note on WhatsApp to yourself each time, then count the categories with a family member at the end of the day.
Memory underestimates small time leaks; a written log shows the truth.

Time Wasters and Energy Drains, and How to Reduce Them
Name the most common time wasters in a busy household and business
Use phone settings to limit distracting apps
Reduce interruptions and repeated trips with simple systems

Your audit has probably shown some leaks. This lesson names the usual culprits and gives a fix for each. You will not remove every waster, and you do not need to. Cutting two or three of the biggest ones can free several hours a week.
A mobile phone
The phone is both a work tool and the biggest time leak for many women; settings can help you control it.
The phone

Your phone is where customers find you, where your children's school sends messages and where family news arrives. It is also designed to keep you scrolling. The goal is not to throw it away but to decide when you use it for what.
**App timers:** Android's Digital Wellbeing lets you set a daily limit per app. iPhone's Screen Time has App Limits. When the limit is reached, the app pauses.
**Bedtime or Downtime modes:** schedule your phone to go quiet and grey at night so you sleep instead of scrolling.
**Turn off non-essential notifications:** keep calls, family and customer chats; switch off group chat and social media alerts.
**Mute busy WhatsApp groups:** open the group, tap its name, choose Mute notifications. Read them once a day at a set time.
**Batch replies:** answer non-urgent messages at two or three fixed times a day instead of every few minutes.
Interruptions and unclear tasks

Each interruption costs more than its own length, because it takes time to get back into what you were doing. Common ones are visitors without notice, children calling 'Mummy!' for things they can do themselves, and calls that could have been a message. Unclear tasks also waste time: 'sort out the house' is hard to start, while 'clear and wipe the kitchen table' is easy.

Worked example: cutting three wasters

For example, Funke sells fabrics from home in Ibadan. Her audit showed 2.5 hours a day on the phone outside sales, about 1 hour a day looking for things, and three market trips a week for forgotten items.
She sets a 45-minute daily limit on Facebook and TikTok in Digital Wellbeing.
She buys two hooks and a box file: keys on the hooks, receipts and school papers in the file.
She sticks a list on the fridge and only goes to market once a week with it.
After two weeks she re-checks: phone outside sales down to about 1 hour a day, searching down to about 15 minutes, market trips down to one.
Funke wins back roughly 2 hours a day plus two market trips a week, which she uses for sales follow-up and an earlier bedtime.
Energy drains

Sometimes the problem is not time but energy. You have the hour but feel too tired to use it. Common energy drains are short sleep, skipping breakfast and then eating heavy food late, not drinking enough water in the heat, a cluttered room that makes every task slower, and unresolved worries that keep the mind busy. Writing worries down, even as a list, often reduces their hold.

Clutter: the hidden time cost

Clutter slows every task: you move things before you can cook, you search before you can dress the children, you clean around piles instead of cleaning the surface. Start small. Clear one surface a day, such as the kitchen counter, the dining table or the top of the fridge. Ask of each item: do we use this? If not, give it away, sell it or throw it away. Keep a box by the door for items going out of the house.
When tiredness does not go away
If you feel exhausted most days even after rest, or feel low for weeks, see a doctor or health worker. Ongoing tiredness can have medical causes, such as anaemia, that need checking.

From Busy to In Charge: Habits of Time Ownership

Taking charge of time is less about willpower and more about a few habits that make good choices easy. This lesson gives you five practical habits used by busy people around the world, adapted for home and small business life.
A woman working with focus at a desk
A protected block of focused time often achieves more than a whole day of scattered effort.
1. Use Parkinson's law: work expands to fill the time

In 1955 the British writer C. Northcote Parkinson observed that 'work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion'. If you give yourself all morning to clean the house, it will take all morning. If you decide it will take 60 minutes and set a timer, it often does. Give tasks a time limit, especially chores and admin.
2. Time blocking

**Time blocking** means giving a task a specific slot on your calendar, like an appointment: 'Tuesday 6:00 to 7:00 am, do the shop accounts.' A task with a time is far more likely to happen than a task on a list. Start with one or two blocks a day, in your best-energy hours.
3. Batching

**Batching** means doing similar tasks together. Reply to all customer messages at 12 noon. Do all the ironing on one evening when there is power. Cook two stews at once and freeze one. Every switch between different tasks costs time, so grouping them saves it.
4. The two-minute rule
Batching also works for errands. Plan one route that covers the bank, the tailor and the pharmacy on the same afternoon, instead of three separate trips across town in traffic.

From David Allen's book *Getting Things Done*: if a task takes less than two minutes, do it now instead of writing it down. Hang the towel, reply 'Yes, I will be there', put the receipt in the file. Small tasks left undone pile up into a heavy load.
5. Habit stacking

New habits stick better when you attach them to something you already do every day. The formula is: **After I [current habit], I will [new habit].** For example: 'After I make my morning tea, I will look at my top three tasks.' 'After I lock the shop, I will write tomorrow's list.'
Worked example: one week of new habits
For example, Chioma is a hairdresser in Port Harcourt with a salon and three children. She chooses two habits for one week.
Habit stack: after she puts the children to bed, she spends 10 minutes writing tomorrow's top three tasks.
Time block: Monday and Thursday, 7:00 to 8:00 am before opening, she orders stock and updates her records.
Batching: she replies to booking messages at 10 am, 2 pm and 6 pm instead of throughout the day.
Two-minute rule: she clears small salon tasks (wiping a chair, filing a receipt) immediately.
On Sunday evening she reviews: the evening list happened 6 nights out of 7; stock was ordered on time both days.
Chioma finishes stock orders on time for the first time in months and feels less scattered, using only about 2.5 hours of planned time a week.

Ownership grows from a small cycle repeated every week, not from one perfect plan.
The weekly review

Once a week, spend 15 minutes answering three questions in a notebook: What went well? What did not happen, and why? What will I change next week? This short review is what turns the habits into lasting change. You will build on it in Module 2.
Paper or phone?

Use whichever tool you will actually open every day. A cheap notebook and pen works well and needs no data or charge. If you prefer your phone, Google Calendar is free on Android and lets you set reminders for time blocks; Google Keep or your phone's notes app is enough for lists. Avoid using several tools at once, or tasks get lost between them. Whatever you choose, keep it in the same place every day so it becomes part of your routine.
If a habit fails for a few days, do not start again from zero in your mind. Simply do it today. Missing one day makes little difference; giving up after one miss is what breaks habits.

Measure progress honestly. A good sign is not that every day goes to plan, but that your most important tasks get done more often than before, and that you end the week with fewer surprises and less last-minute rushing.

Trying everything at once usually fails by Wednesday. Choose the two habits that would help you most, keep them for two weeks, then add another.

The Eisenhower Matrix: Sorting Urgent from Important
Explain the difference between urgent and important tasks
Sort a real task list into the four quadrants of the Eisenhower matrix
Decide what to do now, schedule, delegate or drop
Protect time for important but not urgent tasks

When everything feels like it must be done today, you need a quick way to decide what comes first. The **Eisenhower matrix**, also called the urgent-important matrix, is one of the simplest and best-known tools for this. It is named after Dwight D. Eisenhower, the American general and president, and was made popular by Stephen Covey's book *The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People*.
A person arranging tasks in order of priority
Sorting tasks by urgency and importance tells you which to do now and which to schedule, delegate or drop.
Two questions for every task

**Is it urgent?** Does it need attention now or very soon, with a real consequence if it waits? A customer order due at 4 pm today, a child with a high fever, a bill that will cause a disconnection tomorrow.
**Is it important?** Does it move you towards your goals, protect your family's health, income or wellbeing? Saving for school fees, learning a new skill, checking your business records, rest.

Urgent things shout; important things often whisper. Many urgent things are not important (a ringing phone, a forwarded message asking you to share it now), and many important things are never urgent until it is too late (a health check, a savings plan, servicing the generator).
Do now: urgent, important
Schedule: important, not urgent
Delegate: urgent, not important
Drop: neither

The key insight is quadrant 2. When you schedule important tasks before they become urgent, quadrant 1 shrinks. For example, servicing the generator on a planned Saturday (quadrant 2) prevents a breakdown on the night before an exam (quadrant 1). Buying school uniforms in the holidays prevents the rush on resumption day.
Worked example: sorting a Monday list
For example, Joy runs a small catering business in Abuja and has ten things on her list on Monday morning.
Q1 Do now: deliver the small chops order due at 1 pm; pay the electricity token before tonight; collect her son's medicine.
Q2 Schedule: update her price list (Wednesday 7 am); plan next week's menu (Saturday 6 pm); open a savings account for equipment (Thursday lunchtime).
Q3 Delegate: buying soft drinks for the order (her assistant); replying to price enquiries (copy-paste her saved quick reply once at noon).
Q4 Drop: watching a long video someone sent; joining a new WhatsApp group about a party she will not attend.
She does the three Q1 tasks by 1:30 pm, then puts the Q2 tasks into her calendar with times.
Joy finishes the urgent work early and, for the first time in weeks, has the important but easy-to-postpone tasks booked into her week.
Delegating is not dumping

When you delegate, give clear instructions: what, by when, and what 'done' looks like. For example: 'Please buy 2 crates of Coke and 1 pack of water from the shop before 11 am, and keep the receipt.' Check once, kindly, then trust the person.
Common mistakes
Putting everything in quadrant 1. Ask honestly: what happens if this waits until tomorrow?
Never giving anything to quadrant 3 because 'nobody does it like me'. Accept good enough from others for low-importance tasks.
Treating other people's urgency as your own. A friend's last-minute request is urgent to her; it may not be important to you.
Leaving quadrant 2 empty. Book at least one quadrant 2 task every day, even 20 minutes.
Using the matrix every day

You do not need to draw the full matrix every morning. Once you are used to it, a quick mark next to each item on your list is enough: 1, 2, 3 or 4. Do the 1s first, give each 2 a time, hand over or batch the 3s, and cross out the 4s. Redo the full matrix at your weekly planning session, when you have more time to think.

Remember that importance depends on your goals. Joining a cooperative meeting may be quadrant 2 for a woman building a business and quadrant 4 for someone else. Decide based on what matters to you and your family this season, not on what others think should matter.
Urgent means it needs attention soon; important means it serves your goals and wellbeing.

A plan does not need to be fancy. It needs to be made regularly, kept in one place and flexible enough to bend when life happens. This lesson gives you a simple weekly session and a five-minute daily plan that work together.
A person marking dates on a large calendar
A short weekly planning session places your important tasks on specific days before the week fills up.
The weekly planning session (30 minutes)

Choose a fixed time each week, for example Sunday evening after the children are in bed, or Saturday morning before the market. Sit with your notebook or calendar, last week's notes and your task list.
**Review last week (5 minutes):** what got done, what did not, and why.
**List fixed commitments (5 minutes):** work hours, school events, appointments, worship, deliveries, family events. Write them on the days.
**Choose your 'big rocks' (5 minutes):** the three to five most important tasks for the week, mostly quadrant 2 tasks from the Eisenhower matrix.
**Place big rocks first (5 minutes):** give each one a day and a time, in your best-energy hours if possible.
**Add home rhythm (5 minutes):** market day, laundry day, cooking and batch-cooking days, cleaning tasks.
**Leave buffer (5 minutes):** keep at least one free hour on most days for the unexpected.

The idea of 'big rocks' is often explained with a jar: if you pour in sand and pebbles first, the big rocks do not fit; if you put the big rocks in first, the pebbles and sand settle around them. Your important tasks are the rocks. Small tasks will always find space.

Each evening, or first thing in the morning, look at the weekly plan and write your **top three** for the day: the three tasks that would make the day a success if nothing else got done. Then list smaller tasks underneath. Do at least one of the top three before you open social media.

For example, Aisha works as a nurse on day shifts in Kano (Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday) and sells perfume oils on WhatsApp. On Sunday evening she plans her week.

All four big rocks are done by Thursday night. When her shift runs late on Friday, nothing important is lost because Friday evening was buffer.
When the plan breaks
**Power cut:** swap tasks. Do tasks that need no power (planning, sorting, market) and move ironing or blending to when power returns.
**Unexpected visitors or a family emergency:** move today's top three to tomorrow's top three. Do not try to do everything late at night.
**Sick day:** cancel all but quadrant 1 tasks. Rest is the most important task when you are unwell.
**Task took longer than planned:** note it. Next time, plan more time for that kind of task.
Use reminders

In Google Calendar you can add a reminder to any event, such as 30 minutes before. For recurring tasks like 'pay rent' or 'buy gas', set them to repeat monthly so you never need to remember them yourself.
Keep your plan visible. A paper weekly plan on the fridge also helps your family see what is happening, which makes sharing tasks easier (Module 3).
Planning as a family

If you share a home, spend five minutes of your weekly session with your husband or older children. Tell them the big events of the week, ask what they have coming up (a school excursion, a football match, a work trip), and agree who handles which errand. Writing everyone's commitments on one shared page avoids the Sunday-night surprise of 'Mummy, I need cardboard for school tomorrow'. A shared Google Calendar works well for families who all have smartphones.

Plan your big rocks on days off first, and keep work days for small tasks only. A plan that respects your real hours is better than a perfect plan you cannot follow.

Realistic timelines

Most people underestimate how long things take, because they plan for the best case and forget interruptions, travel, power cuts and waiting for other people. A simple rule of thumb: estimate the time, then add half again. If you think sewing a dress will take 4 hours, plan 6. If you think a supplier will deliver in a week, plan for two. Over time, compare your estimates with the real times you recorded and adjust.
**Choose one or two goals at a time.** Five goals at once usually means none get enough time.
**Check money as well as time.** A goal that needs 200,000 naira you do not have needs a savings milestone first.
**Write down what you need from others.** If your goal depends on a husband, sister or supplier, agree it with them early.
Tracking and adjusting

In your weekly review, check each goal: on track, a little behind, or stuck. If you are behind, ask why. Was the timeline too short? Did something urgent take over? Do you need help or money? Adjusting a date is not failure. Abandoning the goal without asking why is what to avoid.
Goals for the whole family
Goals do not have to be only yours. A family goal, such as 'Everyone in bed by 10 pm on school nights' or 'Save for a family holiday in December', can be agreed together and tracked on the fridge.
Goals and money together

Many goals for women in business and home management are money goals: school fees, rent, equipment, stock, a family emergency fund. For these, divide the amount by the number of weeks left to find a weekly saving target. For example, 120,000 naira over 12 weeks is 10,000 naira a week. If that number is too high for your budget, either extend the date or reduce the goal. A savings group (ajo, esusu or adashe) or a separate savings account can help you keep the money aside, but only join groups run by people you know and trust, with clear written records.
Finally, celebrate milestones. When you reach one, mark it on your plan and tell someone who supports you. Small celebrations keep motivation alive over the weeks it takes to reach a big goal.

The Art of Saying No: Protecting Your Plan Respectfully

Use the pause before answering any request

Your plan will be tested by requests: a relative who needs you to cook for a party, a friend who wants you to follow her to the market, a church committee looking for volunteers, a customer who wants a dress by tomorrow. In many Nigerian families and communities, saying no can feel rude, especially to elders. This lesson is about saying no in a way that protects both your time and your relationships.
A no entry sign
A respectful no protects the time you set aside for your most important tasks.
Every yes is also a no

When you say yes to one thing, you say no to something else in your 168 hours. If you agree to spend Saturday cooking for a cousin's party, you are saying no to your market day, your rest or your sewing orders. Before agreeing, ask yourself: what will I give up for this?
The pause

The most powerful tool is not the word 'no'. It is the pause. Most requests do not need an answer immediately. Train yourself to say: **'Let me check my week and get back to you this evening.'** This gives you time to look at your plan and decide calmly, instead of agreeing out of habit or pressure.

If you decide to say yes, say a full yes. Agree the exact time you can give, write it in your plan, and arrive ready. Half-hearted yeses, where you agree but arrive late or leave early with complaints, often damage relationships more than a kind no.

Notice the pattern: a warm opening, a clear answer, a short reason if you want to give one, and often an alternative. You do not need to give long excuses. Long explanations invite argument.
Worked example: a smaller yes

For example, Patience's aunt calls on Thursday asking her to spend all of Saturday helping prepare food for a naming ceremony. Patience has planned Saturday for her tailoring orders, which are due on Monday.
She pauses: 'Aunty, let me check how my week is and I will call you back tonight.'
She checks her plan: four orders due Monday need about 6 hours on Saturday.
She decides on a smaller yes: she can come for 2 hours on Saturday morning to help with the peppers and onions, then return to her sewing.
She calls back: 'Aunty, congratulations again. I have customer orders due Monday, so I cannot stay the whole day, but I will come from 7 to 9 in the morning to help with the preparation.'
Her aunt accepts and is grateful for the help.
Patience keeps the relationship warm, helps her family, and still delivers her orders on time.
Watch out for money scams that use urgency

Messages saying a relative is in trouble and needs money sent immediately, or that you must pay a fee to receive a prize, use urgency to stop you thinking. Pause, call the person directly on a number you already know, and never share your bank PIN or one-time password (OTP) with anyone.
When it is hard to say no
**Elders:** speak with respect, offer what you can, and if possible ask another family member to share the load.
**Husband or partner:** talk about the weekly plan together, so requests fit into it instead of competing with it.
**Guilt afterwards:** remind yourself that protecting your time is how you keep your promises to customers, children and yourself.

Saying no gets easier with practice. Start with low-risk requests, such as declining to join a new WhatsApp group or postponing a casual visit, and build confidence before the harder conversations. Many women find that people respect a clear and kind no more than a reluctant yes that is done late or with resentment.

Home Management Systems

Good systems mean the home runs without you holding every detail in your head. In this module you design daily and weekly routines, share chores fairly across the household, plan meals and a household budget together, and manage the family calendar of school, events and community commitments.
Designing Daily and Weekly Home Routines

Keep routines simple enough to follow on busy days

A **routine** is a set of tasks done in the same order at roughly the same time. Routines save time because you stop deciding what to do next; the steps become automatic. They also make it easier for others in the home to help, because everyone knows what happens when. This lesson helps you design routines for your real home, including power cuts and water.
A person organising a schedule board

The morning routine

Mornings are often the most rushed part of the day, especially on school days. Most of a calm morning is actually prepared the night before. Keep your morning list short, five to seven steps, and put it in order.
Wake up at a fixed time, ideally 20 to 30 minutes before the children.
Personal time: prayer, a glass of water, a look at your top three tasks.
Start breakfast (prepared or partly prepared the night before).
Children wash and dress; uniforms and bags were set out last night.
Quick tidy: beds made, breakfast dishes soaked or washed.
Leave on time with everything checked: keys, phone, lunch packs.
The evening reset

The evening reset prepares tomorrow and stops mess from building up. Even 20 to 30 minutes makes a big difference. A good evening reset includes: kitchen cleared and pots washed, uniforms and bags ready, a quick check of tomorrow's plan, phones charging, and a 10-minute tidy of the main room with everyone helping.

Batch cooking and safe storage

Batch cooking means cooking large amounts once and storing portions. Follow the World Health Organization's **Five Keys to Safer Food**: keep clean; separate raw and cooked food; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; use safe water and raw materials. In practice:
Wash hands before cooking and after touching raw meat or fish.
Use separate boards or wash them well between raw meat and ready-to-eat food.
Cool cooked food quickly and put it in the fridge or freezer within 2 hours. Do not leave stew out overnight at room temperature.
Store in clean, covered containers in portions for one meal, so you only reheat what you need.
Reheat until steaming hot all the way through, and reheat only once.
During long power cuts, keep the freezer closed. If frozen food has fully thawed and warmed, cook it straight away or throw it away.
Part 2: The household budget

A **budget** is a plan for your money before you spend it. Write your monthly income from all sources (salary, business profit, regular support from family). Then list spending in three groups: **needs** (rent, food, school fees, transport, electricity, water, gas, health), **wants** (eating out, new clothes beyond the basics, data for entertainment), and **savings** (emergency fund, school fees fund, business). A common rule of thumb is 50% needs, 30% wants and 20% savings, but in many Nigerian households needs take more than half. That is fine: the aim is to plan, and to save something regularly, even 5% to start.

Savings: emergency fund 30,000 and business stock 10,000. Total 40,000 (10%).
Wants: data for entertainment, outings, gifts 40,000 (10%).
Check: 320,000 + 40,000 + 40,000 = 400,000. Every naira has a job.
Meal planning cuts their food spending from about 160,000 to 140,000 by reducing waste and extra trips; the 20,000 saved goes to the emergency fund.
Ruth's family knows exactly where the money goes, saves 10% every month, and can see that meal planning pays for their emergency fund.
Tracking spending

A budget only works if you check it. Two simple methods: the **envelope method** (put cash for each category, such as food or transport, into labelled envelopes; when an envelope is empty, that category is finished for the month) and the **notebook method** (write every expense with the date and category, and add up weekly). If you pay mostly by transfer, many banking apps such as Opay, Moniepoint or your bank's app show your transaction history, which you can check each week.
Protect your money
Never share your PIN, password or OTP with anyone, including people claiming to be from your bank. Banks do not ask for these by phone or message.

Buying some staples in bulk, such as a bag of rice, a paint bucket of garri or a gallon of oil, can lower the cost per meal, but only if you have the cash without cutting other needs and somewhere dry and pest-free to store them. Some women share a bag with a neighbour or join a food cooperative to get bulk prices on a smaller budget.

Beyond daily routines, every household has a stream of commitments: school terms, PTA meetings, open days, birthdays, weddings and naming ceremonies, church or mosque activities, cooperative meetings, visits to the village. Many of them are known weeks or months ahead, yet still arrive as surprises. This lesson shows you how to see them coming.
A school bag
School terms follow a known pattern, so resumption costs and tasks can be planned long before the first day.
One family calendar

Choose one place where every commitment is written: a large wall calendar in the kitchen, or a shared Google Calendar if all the adults have smartphones. Use one colour or symbol per person. The rule is simple: if it is not on the calendar, it is not planned.
School: term start and end dates, mid-term breaks, exams, PTA meetings, open days, fees deadlines.
Family: birthdays, anniversaries, visits, medical appointments, vaccinations.
Community: weddings, burials, naming ceremonies, church or mosque programmes, cooperative or ajo meetings.
Money dates: rent due, school fees, levies, contributions.
Prepare early for predictable peaks
Some periods are always busy: school resumption, festive seasons such as Christmas, Sallah and Easter, and the end of the year. Make a checklist for each and start four to six weeks before.

Fees saved or paid
Uniforms and shoes checked
Books and stationery bought
Lunch box and bottle ready
Routines restarted a week early
Starting this list a month before resumption spreads both the cost and the work.
Worked example: planning the September resumption
For example, Grace in Lagos has three children in primary and secondary school. Last year she spent the weekend before resumption rushing between markets.
In early July, she writes the resumption date on the family calendar and sets a reminder for 1 August.
On 1 August, she checks uniforms and shoes with each child and lists what is needed.
She divides the expected cost by 5 weeks and saves a fixed amount weekly in a separate account.
In mid August, she buys books and stationery on a weekday, when the market is quieter.
One week before resumption, the children return to school-day bedtimes and the morning routine.
Resumption morning is calm, everything is ready, and the cost was spread across five weeks instead of landing in one.
Events, celebrations and contributions
Social events are an important part of family and community life, and they cost time and money: aso ebi fabric, sewing, transport, gifts, contributions. Plan them like any other commitment.

Balance, Boundaries and Wellbeing

Plans fail when the person running them is exhausted. This module covers rest and recovery, setting and keeping boundaries, balancing a small business or job with home and family, and building a monthly and quarterly review that keeps your systems working for years.
Rest, Recovery and the Myth of Busyness
Explain why rest is part of productivity, not the opposite of it
Plan for enough sleep and short breaks in your day
Use focused work periods with breaks, such as the Pomodoro technique
Recognise the signs of burnout and know when to seek help

Many women are praised for never resting: first up, last to bed, always on their feet. But a tired mind makes more mistakes, takes longer over tasks and gets irritable more easily. Rest is not laziness. It is maintenance, like servicing a generator so it keeps running.
A woman relaxing on a sofa at home
Planned rest is part of a working system, not a reward you earn only when everything is done.
Sleep first

Health authorities such as the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advise that most adults need **7 or more hours of sleep** a night. Regularly sleeping less is linked with poorer concentration and health. Protect sleep the way you protect a customer delivery.
Choose a fixed bedtime and wake time, even at weekends where possible.
Use your phone's Bedtime mode (Android) or Sleep Focus (iPhone) to silence notifications at night.
Stop screens 30 minutes before bed and keep the phone away from the pillow.
Keep the room as dark and cool as you can; a fan or open window helps in the heat, with a mosquito net.
Avoid heavy meals and strong coffee or tea late in the evening.
Short breaks during the day

Long stretches of work without a pause wear down attention. Short breaks restore it. The **Pomodoro technique**, developed by Francesco Cirillo, is a simple method: work on one task for **25 minutes**, then take a **5-minute break**. After four rounds, take a longer break of 15 to 30 minutes. You can use your phone's timer or a kitchen timer.
The Pomodoro cycle
Choose one task
Work 25 minutes
Break 5 minutes
Repeat four times
Long break 15 to 30 minutes
Short, regular breaks keep focus steady across a long working day.
A good break means actually stepping away: stretch, drink water, step outside, talk with someone. Scrolling social media during a break often leaves the mind just as busy.
Worked example: adding rest without losing output
For example, Mercy makes and sells bead jewellery in Calabar. She often worked from 6 am to midnight and was making mistakes in her orders.
She sets a bedtime of 11 pm and wake time of 6 am, giving 7 hours.
She works on beading in Pomodoro rounds: 25 minutes focused, 5 minutes stretching or water.
She takes a 30-minute lunch break away from her worktable.
She keeps Sunday afternoon free of orders for rest and family.
After three weeks she counts: errors in orders dropped from about 4 a week to 1, and she still completes the same number of pieces.
Mercy works fewer hours, makes fewer mistakes and feels less irritable with her children, with no drop in sales.

Type of rest
What it looks like

Sleep, a nap, sitting down with feet up, gentle stretching
Mental

Social

Creative or joyful
Music, gardening, cooking for pleasure, a hobby
The myth of busyness

Busyness can feel like proof that you are working hard or are a good mother. But results matter more than activity. A woman who rests well and finishes her top three tasks has done better than one who rushed all day and finished none. In your weekly review, measure what you finished, not how tired you are.
Building rest into your week

Rest that is not planned rarely happens, because there is always one more task. Put rest into your weekly plan as a real appointment. A useful pattern is a short daily pause (15 to 30 minutes after lunch or when the children come home), one longer weekly rest (a half-day, such as Sunday afternoon) and a yearly break (a few days around a holiday when the business closes). Tell your family when your rest times are, and ask them to protect them as you protect theirs.

Mothers of babies and small children often cannot get unbroken sleep. In that season, take rest where you can: sleep when the baby sleeps on at least some days, accept offers of help with cooking or older children, and lower your expectations for the house. The season passes.
Signs of burnout

The World Health Organization describes burnout as a result of chronic workplace stress that has not been managed, with feelings of exhaustion, mental distance or negativity about one's work, and reduced effectiveness. If you feel this way for weeks, feel hopeless, or cannot cope, talk to someone you trust and see a doctor or health worker. Asking for help is a strong and sensible step.

Track rest in your weekly review just as you track tasks. If your energy scores stay low for several weeks even with better sleep, look again at your workload and the chores you could share, and consider a health check.
Rest is maintenance that keeps you productive.

Setting and Keeping Healthy Boundaries
Identify where you need boundaries: time, phone, money, space and energy
State a boundary clearly and kindly
Use tools such as WhatsApp Business away messages to support boundaries
Keep a boundary when it is tested

A **boundary** is a clear limit you set about what you will and will not do, and when. In Module 2 you learned to say no to single requests. Boundaries go further: they are standing rules that stop the same requests from coming again and again. They protect your plan, your rest and your relationships.
A woman sitting calmly with her eyes closed
Clear boundaries protect the calm and energy you need for the people and work that matter most.
Five kinds of boundary
Boundary
Example

'I do not take orders after 8 pm.' 'Saturday mornings are for family.'
Phone

Money
'I do not lend money I cannot afford to lose.' 'Customers pay a deposit before I start.'
Space
'My sewing corner is not a place to keep other things.' 'Please call before visiting.'
Energy
'I attend one evening event a week, not every one.'
How to set a boundary
**Notice the pressure point.** Where do you feel resentful, rushed or drained again and again? That is often where a boundary is missing.
**Decide the rule.** Make it specific: not 'I need more time' but 'No customer calls after 8 pm'.
**Say it once, clearly and kindly.** 'From next week, I will take orders between 8 am and 7 pm.'
**Support it with tools.** Set phone settings, away messages or a sign on the shop door.
**Keep it.** The first few times are the hardest. Respond calmly and repeat it.

A boundary is not unkind; it makes you more reliable to the people who depend on you.
Tools that help
**WhatsApp Business:** set business hours on your profile, an **away message** that replies automatically outside those hours, and **quick replies** for common questions such as prices and delivery.
**Do Not Disturb or Focus modes:** allow calls only from chosen contacts, such as family and your children's school.
**A deposit policy:** write it in your catalogue or status so customers know before ordering.
**A visible notice:** a small sign in your shop or on your gate with opening hours.
Worked example: a business-hours boundary
For example, Tolu sells ready-made clothes on WhatsApp from Abeokuta. Customers message at all hours, and she answers until past midnight.
She decides: business hours 8 am to 7 pm, Monday to Saturday.
In WhatsApp Business she sets her business hours and an away message: 'Thank you for your message. Our hours are 8 am to 7 pm, Monday to Saturday. We will reply first thing tomorrow.'
She posts a status telling customers about the new hours.
One regular customer calls at 10 pm. Tolu does not answer, and replies at 8 am: 'Good morning, sorry I missed your call last night. How can I help?'
After a month, most customers message within hours; sales are the same, and she sleeps before midnight.
Tolu's boundary protects her evenings without losing customers, because the away message tells them exactly when she will reply.
When a boundary is tested

People may push back at first, especially if they are used to you always saying yes. Stay calm and repeat the boundary without long explanations: 'I understand. As I said, I take orders until 7 pm. I will be happy to help tomorrow morning.' If you make an exception for a true emergency, say so: 'This once, because it is urgent.' Otherwise, exceptions quickly become the new rule.

With family, boundaries often work best when framed around a shared benefit: 'If I finish my orders by 7, I can sit with you all in the evening.' People accept limits more easily when they can see what the limit gives them too.
Boundaries and your safety

If someone reacts to your boundaries with threats, intimidation or violence, your safety comes first. Speak to someone you trust and seek help from local support services, a community or faith leader you trust, or the police.

Boundaries also apply to yourself. 'I stop work at 9 pm even if I feel I could do more' is a boundary that protects your sleep. Self-boundaries are often the hardest to keep, so write them where you can see them and track them in your weekly review.

Review your boundaries every few months. As your business grows or your children get older, some boundaries need to change. A boundary that made sense with a newborn may be too strict when your children are at school, and a business that has grown may need stricter order cut-offs.

Balancing a Small Business or Job with Home and Family
Separate business time and money from household time and money
Plan work around the family's daily rhythm
Use batching and simple tools to run a home-based business efficiently
Arrange back-up childcare and support for busy periods

Many women in our network combine several roles: mother, wife, daughter, community member, and earner, whether through a job, a shop, a home-based business or selling online. When all these roles share the same hours and the same space, they blur together. This lesson gives practical ways to keep them balanced.
A woman working on a laptop at home
Working from home works best when business time and family time each have their own clear place in the day.
Separate business money and household money

Mixing business and home money is one of the most common reasons small businesses struggle. When stock money pays for groceries, you cannot see whether the business is making a profit, and you may not have money to restock.
Open a **separate account** for the business. Many banks and mobile money providers such as Opay, Moniepoint and Palmpay offer accounts you can open on a phone.
Pay yourself a **fixed amount** from the business into your household budget each week or month, rather than taking money whenever you need it.
Record every business sale and expense in a notebook or simple app.
Keep money for restocking aside before you pay yourself.

A simple test of whether your business is healthy: after paying for stock, transport, packaging and your fixed pay, is there still money left in the business account at the end of the month? If not, look at your prices and costs before taking on more orders.

Money moves from business to home only as a planned, fixed amount, so both stay healthy.
Fit work around the family rhythm

Look at your family's day and find the natural work windows: early morning before others wake, school hours, nap time for small children, evening after bedtime. Put your most demanding business work (production, accounts, important calls) in the quietest windows. Use busy family times for tasks that tolerate interruptions, such as replying to simple messages or packing orders.
Worked example: a home baker's week
For example, Zainab bakes cakes and meat pies at home in Abuja and has two children aged 4 and 9. Figures are illustrative.

Money: customers pay a 50% deposit by transfer to her business account; each Saturday she moves a fixed 25,000 naira to her household budget.
Back-up: her sister collects the children from school on Fridays, her main baking day, in exchange for a cake for her family each month.
Zainab's baking fits into planned windows, she knows her weekly profit, and the children are cared for on her busiest day.
Batching for business

Batching (Module 1) is especially powerful in business. Set an order cut-off day, buy supplies in one trip, produce in one session, and deliver on set days or by area. Post your product catalogue in WhatsApp Business so customers can see items and prices without asking you one by one. Fewer separate trips and fewer interruptions means more output in fewer hours.
Support for busy periods
**Childcare swaps:** take turns with a trusted neighbour, sister or friend to watch each other's children.
**Seasonal help:** hire short-term help for peak seasons such as December or Sallah, with agreed tasks and pay.
**Simplify home tasks in peak weeks:** batch-cooked meals, a lighter cleaning list, more chores shared by the family.
**Tell the family in advance:** 'This is a busy order week; I need everyone's help with the evening reset.'
Name your work hours aloud

Children and relatives respect work time more when they know it exists. Say: 'From 9 to 12 Mummy is working. After 12 we will have lunch together.' A small sign or a closed door helps younger children understand.
If you have an employer

If you work for an employer, the same ideas apply in a different way. Plan home tasks around your fixed office hours, use your commute or lunch break for planning and quick personal admin if it is safe and allowed, and prepare the evening before so mornings are not a race. If you have a side business as well, check your employment terms, keep it entirely outside working hours, and never use your employer's time, phone or equipment for it.

Guilt is common when you try to balance several roles: guilt about not being with the children, guilt about not answering a customer quickly. A useful question is: did I keep my most important promises this week? If yes, you are doing well, even if some things waited.

The quarterly reset (every three months)

Every three months, take a longer session of about two hours, ideally somewhere quiet. Look at your three monthly reviews together. Ask: Which goals did I reach? Which do I still want? What new goal matters now? Which commitments should I stop, hand over or reduce? A good quarterly reset usually ends with one or two goals for the next three months and at least one thing removed from your plate.

If the quarterly reset feels hard to do alone, do it with a friend or with your husband. Each of you reviews your own areas, then you share your one or two goals and agree to check on each other at the next monthly review.

She adds an order cut-off of Thursday so weekends stay lighter.
Her plan for the next quarter fixes the two weakest areas without giving up the business that is going well.
Seasons of life

Your systems will need to change with your season: a new baby, a child starting secondary school, caring for a sick parent, a business growing fast, a move to a new city. In a heavy season, lower your expectations on purpose: fewer goals, simpler meals, more help, more rest. In a lighter season, you can take on more. Both are normal. Finally, share what works. Teach your daughter the weekly plan, show a friend the chore chart, or explain the envelope method at your women's group. Systems that are shared become easier to keep, and they make life easier for others too.

Why this matters
Every week has 168 hours
Nobody gets more than 168 hours
Fixed time: hard to move
Flexible time: the rest, often leaking away
Energy matters as much as hours
Every week has exactly 168 hours. That is 7 days of 24 hours. Nobody gets more.
What differs from one woman to another is how much of that time is already spoken for.
Fixed time is time you cannot easily move. Sleep, your job or shop hours, the school run, cooking the main meal, worship services you attend every week.
Flexible time is everything else. For most women it is larger than it feels, because it leaks away in small pieces of 10 and 20 minutes.
And energy matters. An hour at 6 am after good sleep is not the same as an hour at 10 pm. Use your best hours for thinking work.
Worked example
Ngozi counts her fixed hours
Sleep: 7 hours x 7 nights = 49 hours
Shop: 9 hours x 6 days = 54 hours
School run and market: about 9 hours
Cooking, washing up, laundry: 17.5 hours
Church: about 5 hours

For example, Ngozi runs a small provisions shop in Enugu and has two children. She writes down her fixed hours with a pencil.
Most adults need 7 or more hours of sleep, so 7 hours times 7 nights is 49 hours.
Her shop is open 9 hours a day, 6 days a week. That is 54 hours.
The school run and market trips take about 1.5 hours a day for 6 days, so 9 hours.
Cooking, washing up and laundry take about 2.5 hours a day. Over 7 days that is 17.5 hours.
Church on Sunday and the midweek service come to about 5 hours.
Her fixed time adds up to 134.5 hours. Take that from 168 and she has 33.5 flexible hours. She had believed she had none.
Step by step
Run a seven-day time audit
Choose a normal week, not a festive one
Make a log in 30-minute rows
Fill it in every two or three hours
Be honest about what really happened
Label each block with a category letter
Fill in the log as you go. Do not wait until night.
Memory is not reliable, so a time audit means writing down what you actually did, as you go, for one week.
Step one. Choose a normal week, not a festive season.
Step two. Make a log on a notebook page or phone, in 30-minute rows from waking to sleeping.
Step three. Every two or three hours, stop and fill in what you did in each block.
Step four. Be honest. Write phone, TikTok, or chatting with neighbour, if that is what happened. Nobody else needs to see it.
Step five. At the end of each day, mark each block with a letter. W for work, H for home, C for care, T for travel and waiting, P for phone, R for rest, and S for social.
The key rule is to fill it in as you go. Waiting until night means you forget the small leaks.

Why this matters
Urgent things shout, important things whisper
Urgent: needs attention now or very soon
Important: serves your goals and wellbeing
Plan important tasks before they become urgent
When everything feels like it must be done today, you need a quick way to decide what comes first. Ask two questions of every task.
First, is it urgent? Does it need attention now, with a real consequence if it waits? An order due at 4 pm today, or a child with a high fever.
Second, is it important? Does it move you towards your goals, or protect your family's health, income or wellbeing? Saving for school fees, checking your business records, rest.
Urgent things shout. Important things often whisper, and they are never urgent until it is too late, like servicing the generator.
Four boxes, four actions
1. Urgent and important: do it now
2. Important, not urgent: schedule it
3. Urgent, not important: delegate or batch
4. Neither: drop or limit
The urgent-important matrix gives you four boxes. Box 1 is urgent and important. Do it now, yourself. A leaking pipe, rent due tomorrow.
Box 2 is important but not urgent. Give it a day and a time. Planning, savings, learning, a health check.
This is the key box. Service the generator on a planned Saturday, and it does not break down the night before an exam.
Box 3 is urgent but not important to you. Delegate it, shorten it or batch it. Most calls and messages sit here.
When you delegate, say what, by when, and what done looks like. Then check once, kindly, and trust the person.
Box 4 is neither. Endless scrolling, chain messages, long gossip. Drop it or limit it.
The common mistake is putting everything in box 1. Ask honestly: what happens if this waits until tomorrow?
30 minutes, once a week
Your weekly planning session
Write fixed commitments on the days
Big rocks go in first. Small tasks always find space.
Choose a fixed time each week, for example Sunday evening. Give each step about 5 minutes.
Step one. Review last week: what got done, what did not, and why.
Step two. Write your fixed commitments on the days. Work hours, school events, appointments, worship, deliveries.
Step three. Choose your big rocks, the three to five most important tasks for the week, mostly from box 2.
Step four. Give each big rock a day and a time, in your best-energy hours.
Think of a jar. Pour in sand first and the big rocks do not fit. Put the rocks in first and the sand settles around them.
Step five, add your home rhythm: market day, laundry day, cooking days. And step six, leave at least one free hour on most days for the unexpected.
Worked example
Aisha plans her week
Fixed: four shifts, PTA meeting, family visit
Eye test and restock on Wednesday, her day off
Catalogue post Thursday 7 pm
Market Saturday 8 am, stews on Sunday
Buffer: Friday evening free
For example, Aisha is a nurse on day shifts in Kano who sells perfume oils on WhatsApp. On Sunday evening she writes her shifts, a PTA meeting and a family visit on the days.
She places her big rocks. Her daughter's eye test and restocking go on Wednesday, her day off. The catalogue post goes on Thursday at 7 pm.
Then home rhythm, market on Saturday at 8 am and two stews cooked and frozen on Sunday. And she leaves Friday evening free.
When her shift runs late on Friday, nothing important is lost. All four big rocks were done by Thursday night.

A SMART goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Save approximately 150,000 naira for my son's next school fees by 1 September, putting aside 15,000 naira every week.

Saying no kindly
Pause before you answer
Pause: let me check my week
Ask: is it important to me?
Choose yes, a smaller yes, or no
Every yes is also a no to something in your 168 hours.
Your plan will be tested by requests. The most powerful tool is the pause. Say: let me check my week and get back to you this evening.
Then check your plan and ask what you would give up.
For example, Patience's aunt asked for her whole Saturday, but she had tailoring orders due on Monday. Patience offered a smaller yes, 2 hours on Saturday morning.

Pause, do not rush
Call the person on a number you know
Never share your bank PIN or OTP

Pause. Call the person directly on a number you already know. And never share your bank PIN or one-time password with anyone.

Why this matters
A home that runs without you holding it all
Routines save you deciding what comes next

A routine is a set of tasks done in the same order at roughly the same time. Routines save time because you stop deciding what to do next.
They also make it easier for others in the home to help, because everyone knows what happens when.
Most of a calm morning is actually prepared the night before. That is why the best first routine is the evening reset.
20 to 30 minutes
Kitchen cleared and pots washed
Uniforms and bags ready
Quick check of tomorrow's plan
Phones charging
10-minute tidy with everyone helping
Never mix bleach with other cleaners. Open windows, wear gloves.
Even 20 to 30 minutes each evening makes a big difference. Clear the kitchen and wash the pots. Set out uniforms and bags.
Check tomorrow's plan, put the phones on charge, and do a 10-minute tidy of the main room with everyone helping.
Then spread the big cleaning across the week, one main task a day of 20 to 40 minutes, so Saturday is lighter.
When you clean bathrooms and toilets, never mix bleach, such as Hypo, with other cleaning products. Dangerous gases can form.
Open windows, wear gloves, and store all chemicals high up, in their labelled containers, away from children and food.
Sharing the load
Share chores in three steps
List every task, including the mental load
Match tasks to age and ability
Agree at a 20-minute family meeting
Post a chore chart and review monthly
If one woman carries most of the work, working faster will not fix it. Sharing will.
First, list every task the home needs. Include the mental load, like remembering fees deadlines or noticing the gas is low.
Second, match tasks to ability. Children can do more than we expect, but keep young children away from hot pots, knives, chemicals and sockets.
Third, hold a short family meeting. Let each person choose some tasks first, then post the chart.

For example, Fatima in Ilorin listed 28 tasks. Her son chose dishes and sweeping, her daughter chose setting the table, and her husband took the Saturday market run. Her housework dropped by about 1.5 hours a day.

Why this matters
Rest is maintenance, not laziness
A tired mind makes more mistakes
Most adults need 7 or more hours of sleep
Plans fail when the planner is exhausted
Many women are praised for never resting. But a tired mind makes more mistakes, takes longer over tasks and gets irritable more easily.
Rest is maintenance, like servicing a generator so it keeps running.
Most adults need 7 or more hours of sleep a night. Choose a fixed bedtime and wake time, stop screens 30 minutes before bed, and switch on your phone's Bedtime mode or Sleep Focus.
Results matter more than busyness. In your weekly review, measure what you finished, not how tired you are.
Worked example
Mercy adds rest and keeps her output
Bedtime 11 pm, wake 6 am: 7 hours
Work 25 minutes, break 5 minutes
30-minute lunch away from the table
Sunday afternoon free for rest and family
Errors fell from about 4 a week to 1
For example, Mercy makes bead jewellery in Calabar. She worked from 6 am to midnight and was making mistakes in her orders.
She set a bedtime of 11 pm and a wake time of 6 am, giving 7 hours.
She worked in Pomodoro rounds. 25 minutes focused on one task, then a 5-minute break to stretch or drink water. After four rounds, a longer break. A good break means stepping away, not scrolling.
She took a 30-minute lunch break away from her worktable, and kept Sunday afternoon free of orders.
After three weeks, errors in her orders dropped from about 4 a week to 1, and she still made the same number of pieces.
Boundaries
Notice the pressure point
Decide a specific rule
Say it once, clearly and kindly
Support it with tools
Keep it, calmly repeating it
True emergencies are the only exceptions.
A boundary is a standing rule about what you will and will not do, and when.
Step one. Notice where you feel resentful, rushed or drained again and again. That is often where a boundary is missing.
Step two. Make it specific. Not I need more time, but no customer calls after 8 pm.
Step three. Say it once, kindly. From next week, I will take orders between 8 am and 7 pm.
Step four. Support it with tools: business hours and an away message in WhatsApp Business, or a sign on the shop door.
Step five. Keep it. Repeat it calmly without long explanations. Otherwise exceptions quickly become the new rule.
For example, Tolu in Abeokuta set hours of 8 am to 7 pm. After a month her sales were the same, and she slept before midnight.
Business and home
Keep the two purses separate
Mixing business and home money is one of the most common reasons small businesses struggle. When stock money pays for groceries, you cannot see your profit.
So keep a separate business account, and keep restock money aside.
Then pay yourself a fixed amount into the household each week or month. For example, Zainab, a home baker in Abuja, moves a fixed 25,000 naira every Saturday. Figures are illustrative.
Look after yourself
When to get help
Exhaustion, negativity about your work and reduced effectiveness, for weeks.
Talk to someone you trust and see a doctor or health worker. Asking for help is sensible.
If a boundary meets threats or violence, speak to someone you trust and seek help.
Know the signs of burnout: exhaustion, feeling distant or negative about your work, and getting less done, for weeks.
If you feel this way, feel hopeless, or cannot cope, talk to someone you trust and see a doctor or health worker. Asking for help is a strong and sensible step.
And if someone reacts to your boundaries with threats or violence, your safety comes first. Seek help from local support services, a leader you trust, or the police.
